doc.body:
You are specialising a generic agent roster for ONE project. The roster you produce IS this project's roster: every agent in this run gets its identity from the file you write, and nothing falls back to the generic source if you leave something out.

## What you are given

The canonical roster, verbatim, at:

  __CANONICAL_COPY_PATH__

Read it with your tools. Each key is an agent name; each value is that agent's generic persona — what it does, stated without reference to any codebase.

The project:
__PROJECT_CONTEXT__

This project is mock3, tracking two tickets: MOCK3-1 (riders aged exactly 65 are charged the adult fare) and MOCK3-2 (the departure board omits the final stop). The roster you produce covers two codelines, mocka and mockb, and four already-minted roles: mocka-fares-investigator and mockb-schedule-investigator (investigators), and fare-boundary-engineer and departure-board-engineer (implementers). Ground each canonical agent's specialised persona in whichever of these two codelines and tickets it actually touches — do not blend mocka's fare-boundary work into mockb's schedule work or vice versa.

The codelines it works on:
__CODELINE_CONTEXT__

mocka (/home/bradleyjerome/projects/mock3/mock-a) holds the fare logic implicated in MOCK3-1, including src/fares.ts and its test file. mockb (/home/bradleyjerome/projects/mock3/mock-b) holds the schedule/departure-board rendering logic implicated in MOCK3-2, including src/schedule.ts and totalMinutes(). Treat these as separate codebases: an investigator or implementer working one codeline should not assume facts about the other.

The stack in use:
__STACK__

Both codelines share the same toolchain: TypeScript with vitest as the test runner. Any command an agent is told to run to verify its own work — type-check, run the relevant test file — should be stated in those terms, not in terms of a different stack.

## What to write

Write a JSON file to:

  __OUT_PATH__

of exactly this shape:

{"agents": {"<agent name>": {"persona": "...", "kind": "implementer|investigator|seam", "ancestor": "<canonical agent name>", "derivedFromSha256": "<sha256 of the ancestor's persona text>", "seam": "<the seam this agent enters by — required only for an agent you ADD>"}}}

EVERY AGENT IN THE CANONICAL ROSTER MUST APPEAR. A missing agent is not a smaller roster — it is an agent with no identity at the moment the pipeline invokes it, and the run has nowhere else to look. Do not decide that an agent is irrelevant to this project; you cannot know which seams a run will reach. This includes any canonical agent that has no direct counterpart among the four roles minted for mock3 — give it a persona grounded in mocka and/or mockb as best fits its generic role, rather than omitting it.

## How to specialise

For each agent, keep WHAT IT DOES and replace WHAT IT KNOWS. The generic persona states a role; your version states that same role against this codeline — its language, its frameworks, its layout, the helpers and conventions that already exist, the commands it actually runs. Read the code to find these. An assertion about the codeline that you did not verify is worse than a generic sentence, because the next reader cannot tell which is which.

For mock3, that means: an investigator or implementer persona should name the actual codeline (mocka or mockb), the actual file (src/fares.ts or src/schedule.ts), and the actual test runner (vitest) it will use to check its own conclusions — but only when the canonical agent's role and the evidence you've read both support that specificity. Do not invent a file, function, or command beyond what is given.

Do not weaken a rule while specialising it. If the generic persona forbids something, says a finding must carry evidence, or names a check that must pass, that survives verbatim in meaning — you are changing what the agent knows, never what it is required to do.

KEEP EACH PERSONA AT THE LENGTH THE WORK NEEDS. A persona that lists every file in the repository is not more specialised, it is less usable: the agent reads it before every invocation.

## Ancestry

Each entry names the canonical agent it derives from. For an agent that exists in the canonical roster, that is the agent itself.

If this project needs an agent the canonical roster does not have, you may add one — but it MUST name the canonical agent it is closest to as its ancestor. That is not bookkeeping: an agent inherits its ladder, its tool grant and its output contract from its ancestor, so an agent invented from nothing has no budget, no tools and no way for the pipeline to receive what it returns. For mock3, the four minted roles (mocka-fares-investigator, mockb-schedule-investigator, fare-boundary-engineer, departure-board-engineer) are the clearest candidates for such additions if they don't already correspond 1:1 to canonical agents — anchor each to whichever canonical investigator or implementer agent it most resembles.

`derivedFromSha256` is the SHA-256 of the ancestor's persona text exactly as it appears in the canonical copy you were given. It records what you derived from, so that a later change to the canonical roster is detectable rather than silent.

## Which seam an agent enters by

An agent does not run on its own. It enters the pipeline through a SEAM, which decides its ladder, its tool grant, its output contract and the prompt it executes. For an agent that exists in the canonical roster, the seam is already known and you do not state it.

For an agent you ADD, name the seam in the `seam` field. It must be one the pipeline already declares — you are choosing which existing door this agent comes through, not inventing one. If none fits, the agent you are adding is doing work the pipeline has no place for, and adding it will not create that place.

Omitting it does not leave the question open: the name is matched against patterns instead, and a pattern is a guess about what an agent does based on how it is spelled. That is how an agent named for review came to enter through an inference seam, with another seam's budget and tools.

## What you are not doing

You are not editing the canonical roster. You are not judging whether an agent should exist. You are not writing prompts — an agent's persona says who it is; its instructions for a task live in that task's prompt.
